note: An experiment (GAME_SPEC §13.7, Stage 55; docs/CURRICULUM.md, experiment 34) on data/benches/beer.json: Beer and Lambert's law. Four standards' absorbance at 750 nm against their concentration is a line through zero, its slope the molar absorptivity times the 1 cm path; the unknown is read on it.
title: Experiment: Beer and Lambert's line

steps.title: Your guess
steps.text: Look at the cuvettes: four standards of copper sulfate, 0.020 to 0.080 M, and an unknown. Compare the unknown's blue with theirs, type your guess of its concentration (mol/L) in the field, then click "predict".
steps.why: A prediction made before measuring is kept as you made it: the report sets it beside what you find.

steps.title: The spectrophotometer
steps.text: Pick up the spectrophotometer in the cabinet and set it on the bench, at the left.
steps.why: It shines one colour at a time through a cuvette and measures how much comes out: the absorbance, A = -log10 of the share that passes.

steps.title: 750 nm
steps.text: Right-click the spectrophotometer and drag its wavelength to 750 nm (the -1 and +1 buttons move it a nanometre).
steps.why: Copper(II) in water absorbs red light, more and more toward the infrared: its blue is what is left. 750 nm is near the top of this instrument's range, where copper absorbs most of what it can reach.

steps.title: The blank
steps.text: Pick up the cuvette of water and click the spectrophotometer: it stands in its well.
steps.why: The blank is the solvent alone: what it absorbs, and what the cuvette's glass reflects, are set as zero.

steps.title: Blank it
steps.why: A single-beam instrument compares each sample's light with the blank's at the same wavelength: blank again whenever you change it.

steps.title: The 0.020 M standard
steps.text: Take the water out and set it back on the bench; put the 0.020 M standard in the well. Open the notebook and write its concentration: the label "c" and the number 0.020, then "write". Close the notebook, right-click the spectrophotometer and click "+ A".
steps.why: Each standard's concentration is known: written beside its absorbance, the pair is a point of the calibration line.

checks.text: the 0.020 M standard in its well

steps.title: The 0.040 M standard
steps.text: Take the last standard out and set it back on the bench; put the 0.040 M standard in the well. Open the notebook and write its concentration: the number 0.040, then "write". Close the notebook, right-click the spectrophotometer and click "+ A".
steps.why: Beer and Lambert: A = epsilon c l. At one wavelength and one path, the absorbance rises in proportion to the concentration.

checks.text: the 0.040 M standard in its well

steps.title: The unknown
steps.text: Take the last standard out, put the unknown in the well, right-click the spectrophotometer and click "+ A".
steps.why: Read on the same instrument, at the same wavelength, against the same blank: its absorbance falls on the standards' line.

report.label: copper's molar absorptivity at 750 nm
report.why: In the notebook: x the column c, y the absorbance, fit: the slope is epsilon l, the cuvette 1.00 cm across. NBS measured 10.23 at 750 nm; this instrument's wavelength is within 2 nm of what it shows, where epsilon climbs 0.6 % a nanometre.

report.label: the unknown's concentration
report.why: c = (A - intercept) / slope, from the line through the standards. The eye judges a blue's depth poorly: a prediction by eye is often off by a third.
